questions.stem: What makes a gland an endocrine gland?
options: It sends electrical impulses along nerve fibres straight to its target organs
It stores hormones made elsewhere and never produces any secretions itself
It secretes hormones directly into the blood rather than through ducts
It secretes its products through ducts onto a body surface or into a cavity
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless: their hormones enter the blood and travel to target cells throughout the body. Glands that release secretions through ducts, such as sweat and salivary glands, are exocrine glands.

questions.stem: Which endocrine gland secretes melatonin, a hormone involved in regulating sleep-wake cycles?
options: Pineal gland
Thymus
Parathyroid gland
Adrenal cortex
questions.explanation: The pineal gland, deep in the brain, secretes melatonin, mostly in darkness, which helps set daily rhythms. The thymus secretes thymosin, and the parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone.

questions.stem: The thymus is most active in childhood. What is the main role of its hormone, thymosin?
options: Increasing the rate of glycogen breakdown in the liver
Promoting the maturation of T lymphocytes
Stimulating the release of milk from the breasts
Raising the concentration of calcium in the blood
questions.explanation: Thymosin promotes the development of T lymphocytes in the thymus, linking the endocrine and immune systems. Raising blood calcium is the role of parathyroid hormone.

questions.stem: Which pair of hormones is secreted by the islets of the pancreas?
options: Thyroxine and calcitonin
Insulin and glucagon
Insulin and adrenaline
Glucagon and cortisol
questions.explanation: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets secrete insulin and alpha cells secrete glucagon. Adrenaline and cortisol come from the adrenal glands, and thyroxine and calcitonin from the thyroid.

questions.stem: Which hormone is matched correctly to the gland that secretes it and its main target?
options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone; posterior pituitary; thyroid gland
Thyroid-stimulating hormone; anterior pituitary; thyroid gland
Thyroid-stimulating hormone; thyroid gland; anterior pituitary
Thyroid-stimulating hormone; hypothalamus; thyroid gland
questions.explanation: TSH is made by the anterior pituitary and stimulates the thyroid to secrete thyroxine. The hypothalamus secretes thyrotropin-releasing hormone, which acts on the anterior pituitary rather than on the thyroid.

questions.stem: Which hormone is secreted by the adrenal cortex rather than the adrenal medulla?
options: Aldosterone
Adrenaline
Noradrenaline
Antidiuretic hormone
questions.explanation: The adrenal cortex secretes steroid hormones, including aldosterone and cortisol. The medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline, and ADH comes from the posterior pituitary.

questions.stem: A person's blood calcium concentration falls. Which hormone is released, and from which gland, to correct this?
options: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex
Parathyroid hormone from the parathyroid glands
Calcitonin from the thyroid gland
Thyroxine from the thyroid gland
questions.explanation: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by releasing calcium from bone, increasing reabsorption in the kidneys and increasing absorption in the gut through activated vitamin D. Calcitonin has the opposite effect and lowers blood calcium.

questions.stem: Thyroxine circulates to almost every tissue. What does it do in its target cells?
options: It increases the reabsorption of water by the kidney
It increases the uptake of glucose by liver cells only
It decreases the heart rate and the rate of breathing
It increases the rate of cellular metabolism
questions.explanation: Thyroxine raises the metabolic rate of most body cells, increasing oxygen use and heat production. Water reabsorption in the kidney is controlled by ADH.

questions.stem: Which hormone acts on the adrenal cortex, stimulating it to secrete cortisol?
options: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
questions.explanation: ACTH from the anterior pituitary targets the adrenal cortex, which responds by secreting cortisol. FSH targets the gonads and TSH targets the thyroid.

questions.stem: Growth hormone is secreted in large amounts during childhood. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is secreted by the anterior pituitary and promotes growth of bone and muscle
It is secreted by the posterior pituitary and promotes growth of bone and muscle
It is secreted by the thyroid and stimulates the pituitary to release other hormones
It is secreted by the hypothalamus and acts only on cells of the long bones
questions.explanation: Growth hormone comes from the anterior pituitary and acts on many tissues, stimulating protein synthesis and the growth of bone and muscle. The posterior pituitary releases only ADH and oxytocin.

questions.stem: Which hormones are produced by the gonads?
options: Testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone
Follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone
Oxytocin and prolactin
Cortisol and aldosterone
questions.explanation: The testes produce testosterone, and the ovaries produce oestrogen and progesterone. FSH and LH are made by the anterior pituitary and act on the gonads, which is a common mix-up.

questions.stem: Which two hormones are released from the posterior pituitary?
options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone and ACTH
Follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone
Antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin
Growth hormone and prolactin
questions.explanation: ADH and oxytocin are released from the posterior pituitary, although they are made in the hypothalamus. The other hormones listed are all made and secreted by the anterior pituitary.

questions.stem: How does the hypothalamus control the release of hormones from the anterior pituitary?
options: It secretes releasing hormones that travel in portal blood vessels to the anterior pituitary
It sends nerve impulses along axons that end inside the anterior pituitary tissue
It produces the anterior pituitary hormones and sends them down nerve axons for storage
It releases neurotransmitters straight into the cerebrospinal fluid around the pituitary
questions.explanation: The link to the anterior pituitary is vascular: releasing and inhibiting hormones enter capillaries in the hypothalamus and travel through portal veins directly to the anterior pituitary. The nerve link, where hormones travel down axons, is to the posterior pituitary.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone is released into the blood from the posterior pituitary. Where is it made?
options: In neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus
In glandular cells of the posterior pituitary
In glandular cells of the anterior pituitary
In cells of the adrenal cortex above the kidney
questions.explanation: ADH is made in the cell bodies of neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus and travels down their axons to be stored in the posterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary is nervous tissue that stores and releases the hormone rather than making it.

questions.stem: A tumour damages the stalk connecting the hypothalamus to the pituitary, cutting both the nerve fibres and the blood vessels. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Lower ADH release but normal TSH release
Normal ADH release but lower TSH release
Higher ADH release and higher TSH release
Lower ADH release and lower TSH release
questions.explanation: ADH reaches the posterior pituitary along nerve axons, and TRH reaches the anterior pituitary through the portal vessels, so cutting both links reduces the release of ADH and TSH. Each answer that keeps one hormone normal ignores one of the two links in the stalk.

questions.stem: A person's thyroid gland is damaged and produces very little thyroxine. What would blood tests most likely show?
options: High TSH, because low thyroxine no longer inhibits the pituitary
Low TSH, because the damaged thyroid sends fewer signals to the pituitary
Low TSH, because thyroxine is needed to make TSH in the pituitary
Normal TSH, because the pituitary does not respond to thyroxine levels
questions.explanation: Thyroxine normally inhibits the release of TRH and TSH by negative feedback. When thyroxine is low, that inhibition is removed and the pituitary releases more TSH, which is why a high TSH is a sign of an underactive thyroid.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the control of thyroxine secretion?
options: Anterior pituitary releases TRH, hypothalamus releases TSH, thyroid releases thyroxine
Thyroid releases TSH, anterior pituitary releases TRH, hypothalamus releases thyroxine
Hypothalamus releases TSH, posterior pituitary releases TRH, thyroid releases thyroxine
Hypothalamus releases TRH, anterior pituitary releases TSH, thyroid releases thyroxine
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus secretes TRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete TSH, which in turn stimulates the thyroid. Rising thyroxine then inhibits the hypothalamus and pituitary by negative feedback.

questions.stem: Why is the hypothalamus described as a link between the nervous and endocrine systems?
options: It receives nerve input and responds by controlling pituitary hormone release
It is the only gland that releases hormones in response to nerve impulses
It converts hormones in the blood into nerve impulses for the spinal cord
It is made of gland cells only and receives no nerve input of its own
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus is part of the brain and receives information from receptors and other brain areas, then controls the pituitary by nerve and hormonal links. The adrenal medulla also releases hormones in response to nerve impulses, so it is not the only gland that does so.

questions.stem: Where are the receptors for a lipid-soluble hormone such as cortisol located?
options: In the walls of the capillaries next to the cell
Inside the target cell, in the cytoplasm or nucleus
On the outer surface of the target cell's plasma membrane
In the blood plasma surrounding the target cell
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble hormones diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors inside the cell. Water-soluble hormones cannot cross the membrane, so their receptors are on the cell surface.

questions.stem: What is the role of a second messenger such as cyclic AMP (cAMP) in hormone action?
options: It carries the signal inside the cell after a water-soluble hormone binds the membrane
It carries a lipid-soluble hormone through the blood to the target cell's nucleus
It transports the hormone across the cell membrane into the cytoplasm
It breaks down the hormone once the target cell has finished responding
questions.explanation: A water-soluble hormone, the first messenger, binds a membrane receptor, which triggers production of cAMP inside the cell. The cAMP activates enzymes that bring about the cell's response, so the hormone itself never enters.

questions.stem: Which hormone is water-soluble and acts through receptors on the target cell membrane?
options: Insulin
Aldosterone
Testosterone
Cortisol
questions.explanation: Insulin is a protein hormone, so it cannot cross the lipid bilayer and binds a membrane receptor. Aldosterone, testosterone and cortisol are steroids, which are lipid-soluble and bind receptors inside the cell.

questions.stem: After a lipid-soluble hormone binds its receptor inside a target cell, what usually brings about the cell's response?
options: The hormone is broken down to release energy for the cell's activities
The hormone activates cAMP at the inner surface of the cell membrane
The hormone-receptor complex switches particular genes on or off
The hormone-receptor complex opens ion channels in the cell membrane
questions.explanation: A steroid hormone bound to its receptor acts on DNA, changing the transcription of particular genes and therefore the proteins the cell makes. Activating cAMP at the membrane is how water-soluble hormones act.

questions.stem: Adrenaline produces effects within seconds, while the effects of cortisol on target cells take hours to develop. Which explanation fits their modes of action?
options: Adrenaline enters the nucleus to alter genes; cortisol binds to membrane receptors
Adrenaline travels in nerve fibres; cortisol travels slowly in the lymph vessels
Adrenaline is lipid-soluble and crosses membranes; cortisol needs a second messenger
Adrenaline activates enzymes already in the cell; cortisol changes which proteins are made
questions.explanation: Adrenaline is water-soluble and acts through a second messenger that quickly activates existing enzymes. Cortisol is a lipid-soluble steroid that alters gene expression, so its effects wait for new proteins to be made.

questions.stem: Thyroxine is made from an amino acid, yet it acts like a steroid hormone. Which feature explains this?
options: It is water-soluble, so it binds receptors on the outer cell membrane
It is a protein, so it is made on ribosomes and stored in secretory vesicles
It needs a second messenger, so it acts on enzymes in the cytoplasm
It is lipid-soluble, so it enters cells and binds receptors inside them
questions.explanation: Although thyroxine is derived from the amino acid tyrosine, it is lipid-soluble, so it crosses the membrane and binds intracellular receptors that alter gene expression. Its chemical origin matters less than its solubility.

questions.stem: One adrenaline molecule binding to a liver cell can lead to the release of a very large number of glucose molecules. What explains this?
options: The second messenger triggers an enzyme cascade that amplifies the signal
Each adrenaline molecule is converted directly into many glucose molecules
Adrenaline enters the nucleus and copies the genes for glycogen many times
Adrenaline binds every receptor on the cell at the same moment it arrives
questions.explanation: Each step of the second-messenger pathway activates many molecules of the next enzyme, so the signal is amplified many times. This is why tiny concentrations of water-soluble hormones can have large effects.

questions.stem: Why do target cells respond to a hormone while other cells exposed to the same blood do not?
options: Only target cells have receptors that match the shape of that hormone
Only target cells are reached by the blood vessels carrying that hormone
Only target cells are close enough to the gland for the hormone to diffuse
Only target cells can break the hormone down into an active form
questions.explanation: Hormones reach almost every cell in the blood, but only cells with specific receptors for a hormone can bind it and respond. This is the basis of hormone specificity.

questions.stem: In type 1 diabetes mellitus, why must people take insulin?
options: The liver can no longer store glucose as glycogen after each meal
The kidneys reabsorb too much glucose from the filtrate into the blood
The beta cells of the pancreas have been destroyed by the immune system
The body's cells have stopped responding to the insulin that is produced
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells, so insulin must be supplied. Cells that stop responding to insulin describe type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: How is human insulin produced by recombinant DNA technology?
options: The insulin protein is injected into bacteria, which copy it many times over
Bacterial genes are inserted into human pancreatic cells to make more insulin
The human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria or yeast, which then make insulin
Insulin is extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs and then purified
questions.explanation: The human insulin gene is joined into a vector, such as a plasmid, and placed into bacteria or yeast. The microorganisms express the gene, and the human insulin is collected and purified. Extraction from animal pancreases was the older method it replaced.

questions.stem: People with diabetes once injected insulin purified from cattle and pig pancreases. What is one benefit of the recombinant human insulin that replaced it?
options: It is a lipid-soluble form that can be swallowed instead of injected
It cures type 1 diabetes, so injections can stop after a short course
It acts on the immune system to stop it attacking the beta cells
It is identical to human insulin, so allergic reactions are less likely
questions.explanation: Recombinant insulin has the same amino acid sequence as human insulin and can be made in large, consistent amounts, so supply is reliable and immune reactions are less likely. It replaces the missing hormone but does not cure the disease.

questions.stem: Before recombinant DNA technology, human growth hormone was extracted from the pituitary glands of people who had died. What was a major advantage of switching to recombinant growth hormone?
options: It produced a hormone with a different and more active structure
It removed the risk of passing on disease from donated tissue
It made the hormone lipid-soluble, so it could be taken orally
It allowed the hormone to be made by the patient's own pituitary
questions.explanation: Some people treated with growth hormone from donated pituitary glands developed a fatal brain disease carried in the tissue. Recombinant growth hormone made by microorganisms removes this risk and can be produced in large amounts.

questions.stem: A person with hypothyroidism takes a daily tablet of synthetic thyroxine. What is the purpose of this treatment?
options: To stimulate the pituitary to produce more thyroid-stimulating hormone
To destroy overactive thyroid tissue that is making excess hormone
To block the thyroxine receptors in the body's target cells
To replace the thyroxine the thyroid gland is not producing
questions.explanation: Synthetic thyroxine replaces the missing hormone, restoring a normal metabolic rate. Because thyroxine is lipid-soluble and small, it survives digestion and can be taken as a tablet. Destroying thyroid tissue is a treatment for hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: A person with hyperthyroidism has most of their thyroid gland removed by surgery. Why might they then take synthetic thyroxine for the rest of their life?
options: Too little thyroid tissue remains to make enough thyroxine
Synthetic thyroxine stops the remaining tissue becoming overactive
Synthetic thyroxine blocks the release of TSH from the hypothalamus
The operation leaves the person unable to absorb iodine from food
questions.explanation: Removing much of the thyroid, or destroying it with radioactive iodine, often leaves the person hypothyroid, so they need synthetic thyroxine to replace what the gland can no longer make. TSH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the hypothalamus.

questions.stem: A patient's thyroid secretes far too much thyroxine. Which group of symptoms would they most likely report?
options: Weight loss, feeling hot, and a rapid heart rate
Weight gain, feeling cold, and a slow heart rate
Excessive thirst, frequent urination, and high blood glucose
Low blood calcium, muscle cramps, and tingling in the fingers
questions.explanation: Excess thyroxine raises the metabolic rate, so more heat is produced, energy stores are used and the heart beats faster. Weight gain, feeling cold and a slow heart rate are signs of hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes gene therapy as researched for diabetes mellitus?
options: Removing the genes for insulin from a person's DNA so their immune system stops reacting
Delivering functional genes into cells, often with a modified virus as vector, so they make insulin
Injecting insulin made by genetically modified bacteria into the fat under the skin each day
Transplanting a whole pancreas from a donor and using drugs to suppress rejection
questions.explanation: Gene therapy introduces genetic material into a patient's cells to treat disease. In diabetes research, genes have been delivered so that cells can produce insulin or so that beta cells are protected. Injecting recombinant insulin replaces the hormone but does not change the patient's own cells.

questions.stem: A gene therapy introduces an insulin-producing gene into some of a patient's liver cells. Would the patient's children inherit this change?
options: Yes, because viral vectors insert genes into the sperm and eggs as well
No, because genes inserted into cells are destroyed when cells divide
No, because liver cells are somatic cells and do not form gametes
Yes, because every cell in the body shares the same altered genome
questions.explanation: Changes made to somatic cells, such as liver cells, affect only the treated person, because gametes come from germline cells. Genes inserted into a dividing cell can be copied to its daughter cells, so they are not automatically destroyed.

questions.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes injects rapid-acting insulin before meals and a long-acting insulin once a day. Why might she use both types?
options: The rapid form treats type 1 diabetes and the long-acting form treats type 2 diabetes
The long-acting form stimulates her beta cells; the rapid form replaces lost glucagon
The rapid form is taken orally and the long-acting form is injected to last longer
The long-acting form keeps a low steady level; the rapid form covers the rise after meals
questions.explanation: Synthetic insulins have been modified to act at different speeds. A long-acting insulin mimics the low background secretion between meals, and a rapid-acting insulin mimics the burst released after eating. Her beta cells have been destroyed, so nothing can stimulate them.

questions.stem: Glucagon can be given by injection to a person with diabetes who is unconscious from very low blood glucose. How does it help?
options: It causes the kidneys to reabsorb glucose from the urine
It causes the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose
It causes muscle cells to take up more of the glucose from the blood
It causes the pancreas to release insulin into the bloodstream
questions.explanation: Glucagon stimulates liver cells to convert glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood and raises blood glucose. Increasing glucose uptake by muscle is an action of insulin and would make the problem worse.
